17:37 To this end... To what extent is using AI a skill? I am not dismissing the idea that AI use may become standard as part of a job, but I question to what extent someone using AI will have a competitive advantage as a workplace function. In your own example, you used AI to bridge a skill/labor gap that was specifically not readily available. To that I have no contest, AI will be incredibly valuable to entrepreneurs and hobbyists looking to find solutions for work they need done with no real market to purchase it from among humans. A lot of the AI art that gets made is not art which would have been reasonably contracted. I currently work maintenance - there are some advantages to using AI search and the like, but if anything, AI is more likely to replace the planners and schedulers while integrating production and maintenance scheduling. Getting rid of production managers would ironically be one of the biggest ways to improve productivity. But that is less someone using AI replacing the job and more of a situation where an entire harness environment has been set up to better network an institution's resources. From my end, even in the use of AI for troubleshooting, there's no real skill to learn or apply. Contrast this with, say, setting up my own. AI agent at home that I can actually task with some things and be isolated enough to not have to worry about it randomly deleting my files or gaslighting me by changing the contents of folders and files to match whatever it is up to. Getting something useful and transformative out of AI seems to be more broadly associated with functions not currently operated on by the market. That said, there were entire departments of digital artists who used to do school pictures. They have been replaced with AI, and while there is a human approving the AI image, the interesting thing is that there is no before and after review. So, the original photograph being touched up by the AI is not even looked at. The AI could be making stuff and people up for all the operator knows. So, there are certainly some professions which, at least from a company level, are going to be significantly altered by AI. The people who use those tools might be able to find jobs on the outside serving a different or developing market, but will probably be displaced into other skills and professions - for better and/or worse.

The majour difference between ai and previous technology is that nobody actually knows the process behind how it generates output. An atm machine has fixed limitations that are percievable and we are aware of how they work. THey communicate with the bank via signals. For ai, it is far more unpredictable and this unpredictability is a vast reason its limitations are very unclear. For example, when writing a book it does not really help you streamline the process, it generates the final product for you. Is it a good book?
